proof_summary: Assuming either prime family is finite, bound it by $N$ and apply the hypothesis to $(N+2)!/6=x+y$, obtaining primes $p=6x-1$ and $q+2=6y+1$ with $p+(q+2)=(N+2)!$. The bound makes the appropriate one of $p$ or $q+2$ divide the factorial, so the identity forces it to divide the other prime; primality then forces equality (the unit case is impossible), contradicting $p\equiv5\pmod6$ and $q+2\equiv1\pmod6$.
